meaning: In written Japanese, the masu-stem (continuative form) of verbs and adjectives is used instead of the te-form to link two clauses.

senses.label: Verb linking
senses.meaning: The verb masu-stem shows a sequence or a list of actions. It equals spoken 「〜て」 but sounds concise and formal. 「〜ている」 becomes 「〜ており」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + 、 (行き, 食べ, し, 〜ており)
examples: I get up at six every morning and leave home at seven.
He graduated from university and got a job at a bank.
We are currently investigating the cause and will announce details at a later date.

senses.label: Adjective linking
senses.meaning: The 「〜く」 form of an i-adjective lists two qualities. It equals 「〜くて」. Common in descriptive writing and ads.
senses.connection: i-adjective minus い + く、 (安く, 広く)
examples: This room is spacious and gets plenty of sunlight.
The price is low, and the quality is good too.

senses.label: Nouns・na-adjectives
senses.meaning: 「〜であり」 links nouns or na-adjectives. It equals 「〜で」. The tone is formal; common in papers and speeches.
senses.connection: Noun／na-adjective stem + であり、
examples: He is a doctor and also a writer.
This town has convenient transportation and is easy to live in.

senses.label: Negative linking
senses.meaning: 「〜ず」 means “without doing ...” or lists negatives. It equals 「〜ないで」／「〜なくて」 and has a strong written feel.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form minus ない + ず、 (言わず, 食べず; する → せず)
examples: He left the room without saying a word.
I went to school without eating breakfast.

notes: The gapped form carries no tense of its own; the end of the sentence decides it. In 「六時に起き、七時に出た」, 「起き」 is also past, so don't write ✕「起きた、七時に出た」.
The gapped form of 「する」 is 「し」, and its negative is 「せず」: ✕「しず」→ ○「せず」. The negative of 「来る」 is 「来ず（こず）」.
「〜ており」 is a formal, humble-leaning form, used only for your own side or for neutral reporting such as news. Never use it for a client's or superior's actions: ✕「お客様が待っており、」→ ○「お客様がお待ちで、」.
This is written style. In conversation, 「昨日は映画を見、ご飯を食べた」 sounds stiff and affected; speech uses the te-form: 「見て、食べて」.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A news anchor reports what happened.
daily.example: Last night, a strong earthquake hit Tokyo, and many people were startled.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes a series of a character's actions.
daily.example: She quietly stood up and looked out the window.

work.example: Sales increased over the previous year, and profits also improved.

etymology: The name 「連用形」 means “the form that connects to inflecting words”. In classical Japanese this form could already stand alone to link to what follows. Modern written Japanese kept this use, while speech switched to 「て」.

similar.title: 〜て (te-form connection / sequence)
similar.explanation: Basically the same meaning: sequence or listing. 「て」 is used in speech and ordinary writing; the gapped form drops 「て」, which is more concise and formal, common in news, reports and papers.

similar.title: 〜ずに
similar.explanation: The negative gapped 「〜ず、」 and 「〜ずに」 both come from the negative 「ず」. 「〜ずに」 modifies the following action, meaning “without doing …” (「何も言わずに出ていった」); 「〜ず、」 is more like a pause-and-list, where the two clauses stay fairly independent.

similar.title: 〜ないで (without doing)
similar.explanation: 「〜ないで」 is the spoken form; in writing it is often replaced by 「〜ず（に）」. 「朝ご飯を食べないで学校へ行った」 and 「朝ご飯を食べず、学校へ行った」 mean about the same, the latter being more formal.

formation: 「連用形」 gets its name from “connecting to an inflected word that follows,” and it is by nature a form that says “I'm not done, more is coming.” Put directly before a comma, it leaves the first clause hanging unfinished, to be closed by the next clause, which yields a sequence or listing: “…, and then / and …”. The spoken 「〜て」 is really the continuative form plus the particle 「て」, and the gapped form simply drops 「て」, which is why it feels more concise and written. Likewise, i-adjectives use 「〜く」, the copula 「だ」 uses the written 「であり」, and negatives use the classical 「ず」, giving 「安く、」, 「医者であり、」 and 「言わず、」. Since the continuative form itself shows neither tense nor politeness, both are decided by the end of the sentence.

meaning: Adding 「の」 after a case particle lets a direction, place, starting point, or partner directly modify a noun.
connection: Noun + へ／で／から／と／まで + の + noun

senses.label: への (recipient・direction)
senses.meaning: Means “to ...” or “for ...” before a noun. The noun is often a letter, gift, trip, or thanks.
senses.connection: Noun + への + noun. Common: 「〜への手紙」, 「〜への感謝」, 「〜への旅行」
examples: This is a letter to my teacher.
The number of people traveling abroad is increasing.

senses.label: での (place)
senses.meaning: Means “in／at ...” before a noun. It stresses where an action or event takes place.
senses.connection: Noun + での + noun. Common: 「〜での生活」, 「〜での経験」, 「〜での発言」
examples: I've already gotten used to life in Japan.
Please be careful about what you say in meetings.

senses.label: からの (origin・source)
senses.meaning: Means “from ...” before a noun. The starting point can be a person, a place, or a time.
senses.connection: Noun + からの + noun. Common: 「〜からの連絡」, 「〜からの道」, 「〜からの帰り」
examples: I read the email from my mother.
I don't know the way from the station.

senses.label: との・までの
senses.meaning: 「との」 means “with ...” and 「までの」 means “up to／as far as ...”. They work the same way as above.
senses.connection: Noun + との／までの + noun. Common: 「〜との約束」, 「〜までの距離」
examples: I had forgotten my promise with a friend.
Please tell me the way to the station.

notes: 「に」 cannot take 「の」 directly: ✕「先生にの手紙」→ ○「先生への手紙」; ✕「東京にの旅行」→ ○「東京への旅行」.
「が」 and 「を」 can't take 「の」 either; just use 「の」: ✕「本をの購入」→ ○「本の購入」; ✕「彼がの発言」→ ○「彼の発言」.
Change the particle and the meaning can flip: 「母への手紙」 is a letter written to your mother, 「母からの手紙」 is a letter from her.
「との」 can mean “with …” (「友だちとの約束」) or introduce content (「中止との連絡」 = a notice saying it is cancelled). Check whether 「と」 follows a partner or a content clause.

etymology: Japanese case particles cannot modify nouns on their own. So the linking particle 「の」 is added to turn “noun + case particle” into a modifier, creating compound forms like 「への」, 「での」, and 「からの」.

similar.title: 〜に対して
similar.explanation: 「先生への感謝」 and 「先生に対する感謝」 are close in meaning. 「に対する」 is more formal and often means “directed against” (「政府に対する批判」); 「への」 stresses “toward / giving.”

similar.title: 〜において
similar.explanation: The formal counterpart of 「での」 is 「における」: 「日本での生活」 ≈ 「日本における生活」. 「における」 is common in papers and official documents, while 「での」 is also used in everyday speech.

similar.title: 〜との (quotation modifying a noun)
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are 「と」 + 「の」. Here 「との」 means “with …” (「友人との約束」); the quotative 「との」 treats the preceding content as the content of a message or notice (「中止との連絡」).

formation: The case particles 「へ・で・から・と・まで」 originally connect only to verbs and can't modify a noun directly; what attaches a noun to a noun is the attributive particle 「の」. So the whole “noun + case particle” is treated as a modifier and hung on the following noun with 「の」: 「先生へ（送る）」 + 「の」 + 「手紙」 → 「先生への手紙」. The case particle keeps its meaning (へ = direction, で = place, から = starting point, と = partner, まで = endpoint) and 「の」 only “links,” so 「への」 means “toward …” and 「からの」 means “from …”. 「に」, 「が」 and 「を」 are generally not used this way: for direction, 「に」 gives way to the similar 「へ」, and 「が」 and 「を」 are simply replaced by 「の」.

meaning: Limits the angle of an evaluation: “in terms of ...” or “as far as ... goes”.
connection: Noun + の／plain form (+ という) + 点で（は）

senses.label: In terms of
senses.meaning: Limits the range of a comparison or evaluation. Often used to compare strengths and weaknesses. Adding 「は」 adds contrast: true in this respect, but not necessarily in others.
senses.connection: Noun + の点で（は）. Common: 「価格の点で」, 「品質の点では」
examples: In terms of quality, this product is better than other companies'.
In terms of price, this one is cheaper.

senses.label: In that ...
senses.meaning: A clause explains exactly which point. 「という」 can be omitted. Often paired with evaluations like 「優れている」, 「有利だ」, 「問題がある」.
senses.connection: Plain form (noun・na-adjective + だ) + という点で（は）
examples: Electric cars are drawing attention because they are eco-friendly.
When it comes to being convenient for commuting, this room is the best.

senses.label: Pointing out a feature
senses.meaning: 「〜点が」／「〜点に」 make a feature the topic and then evaluate it: “what's good／bad is that ...”.
senses.connection: Noun-modifying form + 点が／点に
examples: What's good about this plan is that it doesn't cost anything.
There are parts of his explanation that are hard to understand.

notes: Before 「点」 use the modifying form: noun + 「の」 (「価格の点で」); na-adjective + 「な」 or 「だという」: ✕「便利点で」→ ○「便利な点で」「便利だという点で」.
The 「は」 in 「〜点では」 hints “good in this respect, maybe not in others.” Telling someone to their face 「デザインの点では優れています」 can sound like “well, at least the design is fine,” so mind the context.
To point out a problem, 「〜という点で課題がある」 is much softer than 「〜がだめだ」, and more appropriate in meetings and reviews.
In 「時点で」, 「観点で」, 「地点で」 the 「点」 is part of a compound: 「現時点で」 means “at this point in time,” not “in this respect.”

daily.title: Choosing clothes
daily.description: Comparing two items of clothing with a friend.
daily.example: Design-wise, I like this one better.

work.example: In terms of safety, there are still issues to address.

etymology: 「点」 originally means “a dot or mark”. It came to mean “a particular spot or point in something”, so 「〜点で」 means “on this point”, i.e. “in terms of ...”.

similar.title: 〜からいうと・〜からいえば
similar.explanation: Both present a viewpoint for evaluation. 「からいうと」 means “judging by …” (「経験からいうと」), with a standpoint or criterion before it; 「点で」 means “as regards this feature,” often used to compare strengths and weaknesses.

similar.title: 〜上（じょう）
similar.explanation: 「〜上」 attaches to Sino-Japanese nouns to mean “in terms of …” (「法律上」「健康上」), pointing to a domain or norm; 「〜点で」 takes many kinds of modifiers and points to one specific feature.

similar.title: 〜にかけては
similar.explanation: Both mean “in terms of …”. 「にかけては」 is only for praising someone's ability, “when it comes to … nobody beats them”; 「点で」 can be used for any evaluation, including negative ones.

formation: It is built from the noun 「点」 plus the case particle 「で」, with an attributive phrase before it saying which point. 「点」 originally means “a small dot” and by extension a “point, aspect” of something that can be singled out; 「で」 marks scope (as in 「クラスで一番」). Together, 「〜点で」 means “within the scope of this point,” so a comparison or evaluation always follows, meaning “considering only this point.” Adding 「という」 turns a whole clause into the content of “this point” (「環境に優しいという点で」), and adding 「は」 creates contrast, implying other aspects are a different matter. Replace 「で」 with 「が」 or 「に」 and 「点」 becomes a subject or object, giving 「〜点がいい」 and 「〜点に問題がある」.

meaning: Draws a conclusion based on facts or analysis: “it can be said that ...”. The negative 「とは言えない」 means “you can't say that ...”.
connection: Plain form (「だ」 can be dropped after nouns・na-adjectives) + と言える

senses.label: It can be said
senses.meaning: States a conclusion after analysis or explanation. The tone is objective and measured, softer than a flat assertion. Common in writing and speeches.
senses.connection: Plain form + と言える／と言えます／と言えるだろう／と言えよう
examples: This can be called a great success.
Even by world standards, Japanese summers can be called hot.

senses.label: Can't be said
senses.meaning: 「〜とは言えない」 softly denies something: “it's hard to call it ...”, “you can't say ...”. Often paired with 「必ずしも」 or 「決して」.
senses.connection: Plain form + とは言えない／とは言えません
examples: You can't say this method is necessarily correct.
The preparations can't yet be called sufficient.

senses.label: It could also be said
senses.meaning: 「〜とも言える」 rephrases from another angle. 「〜と言えなくもない」 means “one could say ..., I suppose” and is very indirect.
senses.connection: Plain form + とも言える／と言えなくもない
examples: You could also say that failure is the mother of success.
I suppose you could say his opinion is right too.

notes: To say “can't really be said,” use 「〜とは言えない」; the 「は」 highlights the statement being denied. 「〜と言えない」 without 「は」 sounds unnatural and can be read as “can't bring myself to say.”
「〜と言える」 is a grounded, objective conclusion, good for essays and reports. But saying 「あなたの考えは甘いと言える」 to someone's face sounds patronizing, as if you were lecturing them.
「〜と言えば」 means “speaking of …” and changes the topic; don't mix it up with this pattern: ✕「日本と言える、富士山だ」→ ○「日本と言えば、富士山だ」.
When pointing out shortcomings, 「まだ十分とは言えません」 is far gentler than 「不十分です」, and a tactful choice in meetings and reviews.

daily.title: Talking about a friend
daily.description: Discussing with classmates who works the hardest.
daily.example: You could say he's the hardest worker in our class.

daily.title: Talking about a movie
daily.description: Giving a guarded opinion after a movie.
daily.example: I wouldn't call it interesting, but it wasn't bad.

work.title: Writing a paper
work.description: Carefully stating a view in the conclusion of a paper.
work.example: From these results, it can be said that the two factors are related.

etymology: The quotation particle 「と」 + 「言える」, the potential form of 「言う」. Literally “can be called ...”, it expresses a judgment that has grounds.

similar.title: 〜と言ってもいい
similar.explanation: Both mean “you could say …”. 「と言ってもいい」 is a bit exaggerated, like “it's fine to call it …”; 「と言える」 is more objective and calm, a conclusion drawn from facts.

similar.title: 〜と言っても過言ではない
similar.explanation: The strongest, “it is no exaggeration to say …,” mostly used for emphasis; 「と言える」 just states a plain conclusion.

similar.title: 必ずしも〜ない・必ずしも〜とは限らない
similar.explanation: 「とは限らない」 means “not necessarily,” stressing that exceptions exist; 「とは言えない」 means “can't be called,” denying the assessment itself. They often appear together: 「必ずしも正しいとは言えない」.

similar.title: 〜といえば
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are 「と」 + 「言う」. 「といえば」 is the conditional form, “speaking of … (it reminds me of …),” introducing an association; 「と言える」 is the potential form, “can be described as …,” used to draw a conclusion.

formation: It is built from the quotative particle 「と」 plus 「言える」, the potential form of 「言う」. 「と」 packs the preceding content into a single “way of putting it,” and 「言える」 means “can be said,” literally “can be described as …”. Being able to say something implies facts or reasoning behind it, so it expresses a grounded but not absolute judgment, steadier and more objective than a flat 「〜だ」. The negative 「とは言えない」 means “can't be said so” and denies the claim, not the fact itself, so it works as a gentle partial denial; 「とも言える」 with 「も」 means “can also be put this way,” offering another angle.

meaning: Attaches to a noun to mean “... type” or “... model”. Used to classify things, people's personalities, or shapes.

senses.label: Model・version
senses.meaning: Shows a product's model, spec, or size. Common: 「新型」, 「旧型」, 「最新型」, 「大型」, 「小型」.
senses.connection: Noun・kanji element + 型. Common: 「最新型の〜」, 「大型の〜」
examples: I bought the latest model of smartphone.
A large typhoon is approaching.

senses.label: Types of people
senses.meaning: Classifies people by habits, constitution, or personality: “a ... type of person”.
senses.connection: Noun + 型. Common: 「朝型」, 「夜型」, 「血液型」
examples: I'm a morning person, so I go to bed early.
What's your blood type?

senses.label: Style・format
senses.meaning: Shows an activity or structure of a certain style or format. Common in news and business.
senses.connection: Action noun・noun + 型. Common: 「参加型」, 「体験型」, 「都市型」
examples: Participatory events are gaining popularity.
This class uses hands-on learning.

senses.label: Shape
senses.meaning: Shows that something is made in a certain shape. Can also be written 「形」.
senses.connection: Noun + 型（形）. Common: 「ハート型」, 「星型」
examples: I baked heart-shaped cookies.

notes: After a word it is read 「がた」, but 「典型」, 「模型」, 「原型」, 「類型」 and 「体型」 are read 「けい」. The shape words 「三角形」 and 「四角形」 are also 「けい」, not 「がた」.
As a modifier, add 「の」 (「最新型のスマホ」) or form a compound directly (「大型車」); never 「な」: ✕「最新型なスマホ」.
Blood type (「A型だから几帳面」) is a light topic in Japan, but judging people by blood type or as a 「〜型人間」 at work or in interviews counts as prejudice, even called 「ブラハラ」 (blood-type harassment).

daily.title: Talking about daily habits
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about your sleep schedule.
daily.example: I'm a night owl, so mornings are hard for me.

daily.title: Buying appliances
daily.description: Telling your family about something you just bought.
daily.example: I bought a new-model vacuum cleaner.

work.example: Next month, we will release a new compact model.

work.title: News report
work.description: A weather forecast warns about a typhoon.
work.example: A large typhoon is approaching Kyushu.

etymology: 「型」 has the native reading 「かた」 and originally meant a casting mold. It came to mean “a fixed pattern” and “a category”. After another word, the sound changes (rendaku) and it is read 「がた」.

similar.title: 〜風（ふう）
similar.explanation: Both classify things. 「〜風」 means “… style / … -like” (「和風」「中華風」) and stresses atmosphere and appearance; 「〜型」 stresses type, specification or pattern (「大型」「朝型」).

similar.title: 〜的
similar.explanation: 「日本型経営」 and 「日本的経営」 are close. 「〜型」 puts something into a type or pattern and is a noun; 「〜的」 means “having the nature of …” and is a na-adjective, so 「日本的な」 is fine but ✕「日本型な」 is not.

formation: The noun 「型（かた）」 attaches to other words to form compounds and is read 「がた」 through rendaku. 「型」 originally means a casting mold: things made in one mold all look alike, so it extended to “a fixed pattern” and “a category.” After a noun it means “a group sorted by this mold”: 「大型」 is the large kind, 「朝型」 the early-riser kind, 「参加型」 the participatory kind. Because 「型」 is itself a noun, as a modifier it takes 「の」 or forms a compound directly, not 「な」. For shapes, the similar 「形（かた）」 is used and also takes the voiced 「がた」 reading.

meaning: Supposes a situation and follows it with a bad result (〜ては・〜では・〜ていては): “if it's like this, that's a problem”. Also expresses two actions alternating repeatedly: “did X, then Y, again and again”.
connection: Verb te-form／i-adjective 〜くて + は; noun・na-adjective + では; verb te-form + いては; repetition: verb te-form + は + verb

senses.label: Condition → bad result
senses.meaning: Gives a condition and points out it leads to a bad result. The second part is often 「〜ない」, 「だめだ」, 「無理だ」, etc.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + は (〜ては, 〜では); i-adjective 〜くては
examples: If you play games until late at night, you won't be able to get up in the morning.
When it's this hot, I can't get any work done.
If you eat that much, you'll gain weight.

senses.label: 〜ては困る
senses.meaning: Says you don't want someone to do something, voicing a complaint or request indirectly. Common: 「〜ては困る」, 「〜ては大変だ」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + は困る／は大変だ; passive 「〜られては困る」
examples: We'd appreciate it if you didn't park your car here.
You really can't be late for the time we agreed on.

senses.label: Noun + では
senses.meaning: Takes the situation shown by the noun as a premise and draws a negative conclusion. Common: 「こんな〜では」, 「この〜では」.
senses.connection: Noun／na-adjective stem + では
examples: With these grades, passing is impossible.
We can't play the match in weather like this.

senses.label: Casual 〜ちゃ・〜じゃ
senses.meaning: In speech, 「ては」 shortens to 「ちゃ」 and 「では」 to 「じゃ」. Same meaning, casual tone.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + は → 〜ちゃ／〜じゃ
examples: If you drink that much, you'll ruin your health.
Staring at people like that is rude, you know.
If you're this angry, we can't even talk.

senses.label: Keep this up and it's no good
senses.meaning: If a state or habit continues, it will lead to a negative result: “If you keep ..., (something bad will happen)”. The second half is usually negative. It is common when advising or criticizing someone.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + いては + negative result (〜ない・だめだ・困る, etc.)
examples: If you keep playing games like that, your eyesight will get worse.
If you eat out every day, no amount of money will be enough.
If you just stay silent, nothing will get across.

senses.label: 〜ていたのでは
senses.meaning: 「〜ていたのでは」 means the same as 「〜ていては」, but it is more formal and stresses “things can't go on like this”. It often gives the reason why a method must change.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + いたのでは／いたんでは
examples: If we keep doing it this way, it will never get finished.
If we wait for a reply, we won't make it in time, so we'll start first.

senses.label: Back and forth
senses.meaning: Two actions alternate and repeat many times. Often written twice: 「AてはB、AてはB」. It usually describes pointless or monotonous repetition.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + は + verb masu-stem, verb te-form + は + verb masu-stem
examples: I wrote and erased, wrote and erased, and finally finished the letter.
The rain keeps starting and stopping, starting and stopping.
The baby keeps falling asleep and waking up, and crying when she wakes.

senses.label: Every time A, B
senses.meaning: Every time A happens, B follows, forming a habit: “whenever ..., ...”. The second part often shows the speaker's resignation or criticism.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + は + verb (the second part is often in the ta-form or ている form)
examples: Whenever my father drinks, he talks about the old days.
Whenever he had time off, he went climbing in the mountains alone.
As a child, I often got into fights with friends and then got scolded by my mother.

notes: The second clause must be negative or undesirable; it can't be a good result: ✕「早く寝ては、元気になる」→ ○「早く寝れば、元気になる」.
Connection: nouns and na-adjectives take 「では」, i-adjectives take 「〜くては」: ✕「この成績ては」→ ○「この成績では」; ✕「暑いては」→ ○「暑くては」.

「〜ていては」 is followed by “what bad result will happen,” whereas 「〜ていてはいけない」 is a prohibition, “you must not keep…”. They mean different things: 「寝ていては治らない」 (you won’t get better lying around) ≠ 「寝ていてはいけない」 (you must not lie down).
It must be something repeated many times; it cannot be used for a single occurrence: ✕「昨日、手紙を書いては出した」 → ○「何度も書いては消し、やっと出した」.
The 「ては」 in 「〜については」, 「〜にとっては」 and 「〜としては」 belongs to a compound particle and does not mean “if you do that, it's bad.” Don't misread it.

daily.title: A parent warning a child
daily.description: A mother warns her child who stays up late.
daily.example: If you stay up this late, you won't be able to get up tomorrow.

daily.title: Finding it too expensive while shopping
daily.description: Saying this to a friend after seeing the price.
daily.example: If it's this expensive, there's no way I can buy it.

daily.title: Advice from a friend
daily.description: A friend keeps hesitating, so you urge them to act.
daily.example: If you keep hesitating like that, you'll miss your chance.

daily.title: Complaining about a lazy holiday
daily.description: Telling a friend how you wasted a long weekend.
daily.example: During the holidays, all I did was eat and sleep.

work.title: A boss warning a team member
work.description: A boss warns someone who is often late.
work.example: You really can't be late for meetings.

work.title: Quality check
work.description: The quality-control lead makes a call on a defective product.
work.example: With quality like this, we can't send it to customers.

work.title: Proposing changes in a meeting
work.description: Pointing out the problem with the current method and suggesting a change.
work.example: If we stick with the old methods, we can't win against the competition.

work.title: Reporting on development
work.description: An engineer explains a process of trial and error.
work.example: We built prototypes and improved them, over and over again.

etymology: The conjunctive particle 「て」 + the topic particle 「は」. 「は」 singles out the first clause and then passes a judgment on it: when the second clause is an evaluation it means “that won't do”; when it is an actual action it means the action repeats.
formation: Built from the conjunctive particle 「て」 + the topic particle 「は」 (nouns and na-adjectives use 「で」 + 「は」). 「て」 turns the first clause into a condition, and 「は」 picks that condition out as a topic, roughly “as for doing this...”. Singling out a way of acting as a topic is usually a prelude to rejecting it, so the second clause naturally takes a negative judgment such as 「困る」, 「だめだ」 or 「無理だ」, giving “if it's like this, it's bad”. Adding 「いる」 gives 「〜ていては」, where the condition becomes “keeping on like this”; in speech 「ては」 and 「では」 contract to 「ちゃ」 and 「じゃ」. When the second clause is not a judgment but an action that actually happens, the same 「AてはB」 reads as “A, and then right away B”, and saying it twice (「AてはB、AてはB」) conveys back-and-forth repetition. So these senses are one structure: a first action singled out by 「は」, followed by either an evaluation (a bad result) or the next action (repetition).

similar.title: 〜ようでは
similar.explanation: Both mean “that won't do.” 「ようでは」 usually follows a state the speaker disapproves of, with a critical, scolding tone (「こんなミスをするようでは困る」); 「ては」 is more neutral.

similar.title: 〜たら
similar.explanation: 「たら」 is a neutral conditional, and the main clause can be good or bad; 「ては」 allows only a negative result and carries the judgment “that won't do.”

similar.title: 〜てはいけない
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are 「て」 + 「は」. 「てはいけない」 has become a fixed prohibition, “you must not …”; here the main clause can be any negative result such as 「困る」, 「無理だ」 or 「できない」.

similar.title: 〜たり〜たりする
similar.explanation: Both can describe several actions alternating. 「〜たり〜たり」 merely lists, without regard to order or number; 「〜ては」 stresses that the pair “A, followed immediately by B” is repeated again and again, often with a sense of futility or monotony.

similar.title: 〜たびに
similar.explanation: Close in meaning to “every time ..., ...”. 「〜たびに」 attaches to the dictionary form or 「noun + の」 and objectively states “whenever X happens”; 「〜ては」 attaches only to the te-form and mostly describes habitual repetition, often with the speaker's resignation or criticism.

meaning: You can't avoid doing something because of duty, personal obligations, or common sense. Like “can't not ...” or “have to ...”.
connection: Verb nai-form + わけにはいかない

senses.label: Must, out of obligation
senses.meaning: You may not want to, but given relationships, your position, or common sense, you have to. It carries a feeling of “there's no way around it”.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + わけにはいかない／いきません
examples: It's the wedding of a senior who has done so much for me, so I can't not go.
Everyone is helping, so I can't be the only one who doesn't.

senses.label: Forced by circumstances
senses.meaning: Because of the objective situation, you have no choice but to act.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + わけにはいかなかった (past), etc.
examples: The car broke down, so I have to take it in for repairs.
It was an important exam, so I couldn't skip it.

senses.label: Can't very well not ...
senses.meaning: Adding 「も」, 「〜ないわけにもいかない」 means “I'm not keen, but I can't very well refuse”, with stronger hesitation.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + わけにもいかない
examples: When someone asks me directly, I can't very well say no.

notes: With or without 「ない」 the meaning is opposite: 「行かないわけにはいかない」 = can't not go (must go); 「行くわけにはいかない」 = can't go.

It carries a reluctant feel: “I don't want to, but it'd be improper not to.” If you answer an invitation with 「行かないわけにはいきませんね」, the other person hears you aren't keen; to sound happy to come, say 「ぜひ伺います」.
To simply state a rule or law, use 「〜なければならない」; this pattern adds an unwilling nuance.
It can't be used for feelings or bodily reactions you can't control: ✕「おかしくて笑わないわけにはいかない」→ ○「笑わずにはいられない」.

daily.title: A friend is moving
daily.description: A friend asks everyone to help with the move.
daily.example: It's my friend's move, so I have to help.

daily.title: Eating food someone made
daily.description: A friend went to the trouble of cooking something you don't really like.
daily.example: They went to the trouble of making it, so I can't not eat it.

work.title: A boss invites you out
work.description: The department manager invites you to a drinking party, and it's hard to say no.
work.example: If the department manager invites you, you can't not go to the party.

work.title: Handling a client request
work.description: A client makes an urgent request.
work.example: It's a request from a client, so we have to deal with it.

etymology: 「わけ（訳）」 means “reason／logic” and 「いかない（行かない）」 means “doesn't work”. 「〜ないわけにはいかない」 is literally “the logic of not doing it doesn't work”, using a double negative to mean “must do”.

similar.title: 〜わけにはいかない
similar.explanation: Same origin, opposite direction: after the dictionary form it means “(for reasons of propriety) can't do”; after the nai-form it is this pattern, “can't not do.”

similar.title: 〜なければならない
similar.explanation: Both mean “must.” 「なければならない」 is a general duty or rule with no emotion; this pattern stresses psychological pressure from social obligation or one's position, with a reluctant feel.

similar.title: 〜ざるを得ない
similar.explanation: Both mean “have no choice but to.” 「ざるを得ない」 is more literary and stresses that objectively there is no other option; this pattern is more colloquial and stresses “it wouldn't be right not to.”

similar.title: 〜ずにはいられない
similar.explanation: 「ずにはいられない」 is emotional, “can't help doing” (「笑わずにはいられない」); this pattern is rational, “feeling I have to do it.”

formation: It is built from 「ない」 + the formal noun 「わけ（訳）」 (reason) + 「には」 + 「いかない」 (won't go). 「〜わけにはいかない」 by itself means “doing … doesn't work out reasonably,” i.e. “can't do it”; put 「ない」 in front and it becomes “not doing … doesn't work out reasonably.” A double negative is positive, so it means “must do.” The basis of judgment is 「わけ」 (reason, propriety), not rules or ability, so it stresses that “not doing it wouldn't be right” on grounds of feeling, position or common sense, with a reluctant, resigned tone. Changing 「は」 to 「も」 (「わけにもいかない」) means “it's also awkward not to,” with more hesitation.

meaning: A past action leads to discovering a situation, or to something unexpected happening. Like “when I did ..., I found ...”.
connection: Verb ta-form + ら／verb dictionary form + と, with the second part in the past tense

senses.label: Discovery
senses.meaning: After doing something, you find a situation that already existed. The second part is often 「〜ていた」 or 「〜だった」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ら、〜ていた／verb dictionary form + と、〜ていた
examples: When I got home, the package had arrived.
When I opened the window, it was snowing.

senses.label: Trigger → result
senses.meaning: After doing something, a result immediately follows. The result is beyond the speaker's control.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ら、〜た／verb dictionary form + と、〜た
examples: When I took the medicine, my fever went down right away.
When I pressed the button, the door opened.

senses.label: 〜てみたら
senses.meaning: 「〜てみたら／〜てみると」 means you found out only after trying. It often carries surprise.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + みたら、〜た／みると、〜た
examples: When I went there, the shop was closed.
When I tried it, it was surprisingly good.

notes: The second clause must be a fact or discovery outside the speaker's control, not a deliberate action: ✕「家に帰ったら、勉強した」→ ○「家に帰ってから、勉強した」.
In 「〜と〜た」 the first clause takes the dictionary form, not the past: ✕「窓を開けたと、雪が降っていた」→ ○「窓を開けると、雪が降っていた」.
When the same subject performs two deliberate actions in a row, only 「と」 works (narrative style): ○「彼は部屋に入ると、電気をつけた」; ✕「彼は部屋に入ったら、電気をつけた」.
This “discovery” use can't be swapped for 「ば」 or 「なら」: ✕「家に帰れば、荷物が届いていた」.

daily.title: Waking up
daily.description: Describing to your family what you saw in the morning.
daily.example: When I got up this morning, everything outside was white with snow.

daily.title: Going back home
daily.description: Describing a visit to your parents' home.
daily.example: When I went home for the first time in ages, my mother had cooked a meal and was waiting for me.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describes what happened to the main character.
daily.example: When I opened the door, a man I didn't know was standing there.

work.title: Checking email
work.description: Reporting to your boss that a reply came in.
work.example: When I checked my email, there was a reply from the client.

work.title: Checking data
work.description: Reporting a problem found during a check.
work.example: When I looked into it, I found an error in the data.

etymology: 「たら」 is generally thought to come from the classical 「たらば」 (the irrealis form of the perfective auxiliary 「たり」 + 「ば」). 「と」 is a conditional conjunctive particle. When followed by the past tense, both shift from a hypothesis to narrating an established fact.

similar.title: 〜たところ (result)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both express a result or discovery after doing something. 「たところ」 is more formal, common in reports and business; 「たら」 is more colloquial, and 「と」 is common in narration.

similar.title: 〜と (conditional)
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are the conditional 「と」. The conditional 「と」 expresses an inevitable result or regularity (「春になると花が咲く」), usually with a present-tense main clause; this use has a one-time past event in the main clause.

similar.title: 〜たら
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are 「たら」. Ordinary 「たら」 is hypothetical, with a main clause usually about the future or the speaker's will; this use has a past fact in the main clause, expressing a discovery or result.

formation: It is built from the conditional particle 「たら」 or 「と」 plus a past-tense main clause. 「たら」 originally means “after (if) …,” and 「と」 means “as soon as …”; both treat the first clause as the trigger for the second. When the main clause is in the past and narrates something that happened, it is no longer a hypothesis: it becomes “after the first event, the second turned up right away.” If the main clause is a state like 「〜ていた」 or 「〜だった」, it expresses that after doing the first thing you “saw / discovered” a state that already existed; if it is an action, it is a result triggered by the first clause. Because the main clause is something the speaker comes across, it can't be a deliberate action by the speaker.

meaning: At the end of a sentence, it half-jokingly suggests a possibility: “maybe ...!” or “don't tell me ...”.
connection: Verb・adjective ta-form + りして (noun・na-adjective 〜だったりして)

senses.label: Light guess
senses.meaning: Casually throws out a possibility without being sure. The tone is relaxed, like “maybe ..., who knows”.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + りして; 〜てたりして (〜ていたりして)
examples: Those two... maybe they're actually dating.
Maybe it'll snow tomorrow, who knows.

senses.label: Joking
senses.meaning: Says something unlikely, knowing it's a joke. Often followed by 「なんて」 or 「なーんて」.
senses.connection: Verb・noun 〜だった + りして
examples: Maybe I'm actually a genius.
What if I win the lottery? Ha ha.

senses.label: Worried guess
senses.meaning: Voices a possible bad outcome with some anxiety. The end is often drawn out or trails off with 「……」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + りして……
examples: Don't tell me I dropped my wallet...
What if the trains have stopped?

notes: It is very casual spoken Japanese, for friends, family or online chat. Using it to speculate in business emails or meetings sounds flippant; use 「〜かもしれません」 or 「〜可能性があります」 instead.
Don't joke about someone else's misfortune: saying 「試験、落ちてたりして」 to the person involved sounds gloating and rude.
Even for future events, the ta-form comes first: ✕「明日、雪が降るりして」→ ○「明日、雪が降ったりして」.
In 「本を読んだりして過ごした」 another verb follows 「たりして」, so it is a list (「〜たり〜たりする」). It is this pattern only when it ends the sentence and the rest is left unsaid.

daily.title: Gossiping with a friend
daily.description: Whispering with a close friend about two classmates.
daily.example: Those two... maybe they're going out.

daily.title: Worrying about the weather
daily.description: Looking at the sky before going out and saying this to family.
daily.example: What if the rain never stops...

daily.title: Teasing yourself
daily.description: Joking when a friend compliments you.
daily.example: Maybe I could become a model, ha ha.

work.title: Chatting with coworkers
work.description: Coworkers casually chat about the boss over lunch, in private.
work.example: The department manager is in a good mood today. Maybe something good happened.

etymology: It is generally thought to come from the listing particle 「たり」 + 「して」. Originally 「〜たりして……」 gave one example; once the rest of the sentence was dropped, only one possibility remained, which gave rise to the sense of a light guess.

similar.title: 〜かもしれない
similar.explanation: Both mean “maybe.” 「かもしれない」 is ordinary speculation, usable in formal settings; 「たりして」 is more casual, with a joking or teasing flavor.

similar.title: もしかしたら〜かもしれない
similar.explanation: 「もしかしたら〜かもしれない」 seriously raises a possibility; 「〜たりして」 is lighter, more of a passing remark that the speaker doesn't fully believe.

similar.title: 〜たり〜たりする
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are the listing 「たり」. 「〜たり〜たりする」 lists several actions; this use gives just one possibility, leaves the second half unsaid, and ends the sentence as speculation.

formation: It is built from the listing particle 「たり」 plus 「して」, the te-form of 「する」, and originally was 「〜たりして（……）」: “doing something like …, (and then …).” 「たり」 gives just one example, hinting that other things are possible, and what follows 「して」 is left unsaid, so the sentence stops at “for example, something like that.” Giving one example and not finishing creates an uncertain “it might be so” feel, and so it became a gentle, half-joking speculation. Because it keeps the form of 「たり」, the preceding verb must be in the ta-form even when the event is in the future.

meaning: Judging from signs, “if it looks like ... happens”, followed by a countermeasure, suggestion, or request.
connection: Verb・i-adjective plain form／na-adjective + な／noun + の + ようなら

senses.label: If it looks like ...
senses.meaning: Supposes a situation that seems likely and suggests how to deal with it. The second part is usually advice, a request, or an intention.
senses.connection: Plain form + ようなら. Common: 「〜ないようなら」, 「〜るようなら」
examples: If your fever doesn't go down, you should go to the hospital.
If it looks like you'll be late, please let me know.

senses.label: 〜ようだったら
senses.meaning: In speech, 「〜ようだったら」 is common. Same meaning, more casual.
senses.connection: Plain form + ようだったら
examples: If the rain gets heavier, let's call off the game.
If you're sleepy, go ahead and go to bed.

senses.label: 〜ようであれば
senses.meaning: In formal settings, use 「〜ようであれば」 or 「〜ようでしたら」. Common in business and notices.
senses.connection: Plain form + ようであれば／ようでしたら
examples: If the date is inconvenient for you, we will change the schedule.
If you have any questions, please feel free to contact us.

notes: The second clause is usually a suggestion, request or countermeasure, not a plain result: ✕「雨が降るようなら、道が濡れる」→ ○「雨が降るようなら、傘を持って行こう」.
Connection: nouns take 「の」, na-adjectives take 「な」: ✕「雨ようなら」→ ○「雨のようなら」; ✕「無理ようなら」→ ○「無理なようなら」.
「ご都合が悪いようなら」 sounds a bit casual to a client; in business, 「ご都合が悪いようでしたら」 or 「〜ようであれば」 is more fitting.
「ようなら」 assumes “depending on how things look, based on signs.” If the other person has clearly said they'll be late, 「遅れるなら」 is more natural.

daily.title: Looking after family
daily.description: A mother speaks to her child who has a cold.
daily.example: If you're not feeling well, stay home from school today.

daily.title: Arranging a pickup
daily.description: Making a plan with family on a rainy day.
daily.example: If the rain gets heavier, I'll come pick you up.

work.title: Customer service notice
work.description: A company adds a note at the end of an email to customers.
work.example: If you have any questions, please feel free to contact us.

work.title: Project management
work.description: A boss tells the team to report risks early.
work.example: If it looks like you won't make the deadline, please talk to me early.

etymology: The conditional form 「ようなら（ば）」 of the auxiliary 「ようだ」, which expresses likeness. 「よう」 comes from 「様」 (appearance), so it carries a guess: “if it looks like ...”.

similar.title: 〜なら
similar.explanation: 「なら」 takes something directly as a premise; 「ようなら」 means “if things turn out that way, judging by the situation,” which includes speculation and is gentler. The 「なら」 in 「ようなら」 is this same 「なら」.

similar.title: 〜たら
similar.explanation: 「たら」 is an ordinary conditional; 「ようなら」 stresses a situation judged from signs, and the main clause is usually a countermeasure or suggestion.

similar.title: 〜場合は
similar.explanation: 「〜場合は」 is an objective, formal statement of conditions, common in regulations and notices; 「ようなら」 carries the speaker's guess and concern, mostly when advising a specific person.

similar.title: 〜ようでは
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are 「ようだ」 + conditional. After 「ようでは」 comes a negative judgment (“that won't do”); after 「ようなら」 comes a way to deal with it.

formation: It is built from 「ようなら（ば）」, the conditional form of the comparative auxiliary 「ようだ」 (“it seems”), where 「なら」 is the conditional form of 「だ」. 「ようだ」 expresses a judgment from signs, and 「なら」 expresses a condition, together meaning “if it looks like that.” Because the premise is only “signs,” not established fact, the main clause naturally holds a countermeasure, suggestion or request, and the tone is gentler than using 「なら」 directly. Replacing 「なら」 with 「だったら」, 「であれば」 or 「でしたら」 changes only politeness and register; the structure is identical.

meaning: 「〜かと思う」 offers a judgment softly; 「〜かと思った」 means “I thought ... (but it wasn't so)” or expresses surprise with exaggeration.
connection: Plain form (「だ」 can be dropped after nouns・na-adjectives) + かと思う／かと思った

senses.label: Soft judgment
senses.meaning: States your view in question form, sounding modest rather than assertive. 「〜かと思います」 is common in business.
senses.connection: Plain form + かと思います; 〜のではないかと思う
examples: I think this plan may cost a bit too much.
I think it might rain tomorrow.

senses.label: I thought ...
senses.meaning: 「〜かと思った」 means you thought so at the time, but it wasn't true: “I thought ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form + かと思った／かと思っていた
examples: I thought you'd already gone home.
I was sure I was going to get scolded.

senses.label: Exaggerated surprise
senses.meaning: 「〜かと思った」 exaggerates a strong feeling at the time: “I thought I was going to ...”, “I nearly ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + かと思った. Common: 「死ぬかと思った」
examples: I was so scared I thought I was going to die.
I thought my heart was going to stop!

senses.label: Disapproval
senses.meaning: 「どうかと思う」 politely shows disagreement or doubt: “I'm not sure that's OK”.
senses.connection: 〜は どうかと思う
examples: I'm not sure that's a good way to put it.

notes: 「〜かと思います」 is good for offering opinions gently, especially to disagree with a superior. But with a definite fact (「明日は月曜日かと思います」) it sounds unsure and irresponsible.
「〜かと思った」 means “I thought … (but it wasn't so)” and differs from 「〜と思った」: 「怒られるかと思った」 implies you weren't scolded; 「怒られると思った」 is just what you expected at the time.
「どうかと思う」 is a polite negative judgment, but saying 「部長の案はどうかと思います」 to a superior is still clear criticism, so use it carefully.
「〜かと思うと」 and 「〜かと思ったら」 (N2) mean “no sooner than …”: 「帰ったかと思ったら、また来た」 = he'd just left and came right back, not “I thought he'd left.”

daily.title: Getting a fright
daily.description: A family member suddenly appears behind you.
daily.example: You scared me! I thought you were a burglar.

daily.title: An unexpected encounter
daily.description: You thought your friend was already asleep.
daily.example: You're still up? I thought you'd gone to bed.

work.title: Giving an opinion in a meeting
work.description: Softly pointing out that the materials need changes.
work.example: I think this point may need revising.

work.title: Proposing a date
work.description: Suggesting a time to a client by email.
work.example: I think next week might be better. How does that sound?

etymology: The question particle 「か」 + the quotation particle 「と」 + 「思う」. The judgment is put forward as a question, so it sounds uncertain and soft.

similar.title: 〜と思う (I think)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「かと思う」 is 「と思う」 with the question particle 「か」 added. 「と思う」 states your view directly; with 「か」 it takes on a questioning tone and becomes gentler and more modest.

similar.title: 〜のではないだろうか
similar.explanation: Both offer a view gently in question form. 「のではないだろうか」 is more written, common in essays and speeches; 「かと思います」 is common in spoken business and emails.

similar.title: 〜かと思うと・〜かと思ったら
similar.explanation: Same origin: almost identical in form. The N2 「かと思うと／かと思ったら」 means “no sooner than …,” two events in quick succession; this pattern is a gentle judgment or “I thought …”.

similar.title: 〜と思いきや／〜かと思いきや
similar.explanation: Both mean “I thought … (but not so).” 「思いきや」 is literary, with a slightly classical tone, and must be followed by the surprising outcome; 「かと思った」 is colloquial, and the outcome is often left unsaid.

formation: It is built from the question particle 「か」 + the quotative 「と」 + 「思う」. 「か」 turns the preceding content into a question, and 「と思う」 voices that question as your own thought, literally “thinking ‘I wonder if …’.” Wrapping a judgment in a question makes it less assertive, which is why 「〜かと思います」 became a way to give opinions gently. In the past, 「〜かと思った」 means “I suspected so at the time,” which implies it wasn't actually so, hence “I thought …”; if the suspicion was exaggerated, as in 「死ぬか」, it becomes an expression of strong surprise.

meaning: Humble language meaning “to have the other person kindly do ... for us”. More formal than 「〜ていただく」.
connection: お + verb masu-stem + いただく; ご + Sino-Japanese action noun + いただく

senses.label: Having someone kindly do
senses.meaning: The other person does the action and our side benefits. Used to thank someone or explain what they did for you. Often followed by 「ありがとうございます」.
senses.connection: お〜いただく／ご〜いただく; 〜いただき、ありがとうございます
examples: Thank you all for coming today.
Our teacher was kind enough to come.

senses.label: Polite request
senses.meaning: 「〜いただけますか／いただけませんか」 is a very polite request. Used with customers, bosses, and clients.
senses.connection: お〜いただけますか／ご〜いただけないでしょうか
examples: Could you wait a moment, please?
Could you write your name here, please?

senses.label: Wish・request
senses.meaning: 「〜いただきたい」 and 「〜いただければ幸いです」 softly express that you want someone to do something. Common in letters and emails.
senses.connection: お〜いただきたい／ご〜いただければ幸いです
examples: We would appreciate it if you could check the materials.
We would very much like you to attend.

notes: The most common keigo mistake is mixing 「ご〜いただく」 and 「ご〜する」: ✕「ご説明していただく」→ ○「ご説明いただく」 or 「説明していただく」.
The doer is the other person: 「ご連絡いただく」 means they contact me; when I contact them, say 「ご連絡いたします」. Reverse the direction and the meaning flips.
Native Japanese verbs take 「お」, Sino-Japanese action nouns take 「ご」: ✕「お確認いただく」→ ○「ご確認いただく」. 「お電話」 and 「お返事」 are common exceptions.
The 「いただく」 in 「お菓子をいただく」 is the humble “receive / eat” and is not this pattern. The test is whether 「お／ご＋action」 comes before it.

daily.title: At a shop
daily.description: A clerk asks a customer to wait.
daily.example: Could you wait a moment, please?

daily.title: Wedding speech
daily.description: The groom thanks the guests at the reception.
daily.example: Thank you all for taking time out of your busy schedules to be here today.

work.title: Requesting a check by email
work.description: Sending materials to a client and asking them to check.
work.example: Could you please check the attached materials?

work.title: Thanks at the end of a project
work.description: Thanking a partner after a project is finished.
work.example: Thank you very much for your tremendous cooperation.

etymology: 「いただく」 is written 「頂く・戴く」 and originally meant “to place on top of one's head”. From respectfully raising something above one's head to receive it, it came to be a humble verb for “to receive”. Combined with 「お／ご + masu-stem」, it forms an even more formal humble expression.

similar.title: 〜ていただく
similar.explanation: Same meaning: “I received the favor of the other person doing it.” 「ていただく」 attaches to almost any verb; 「お〜いただく」 is more formal, common in reception and business.

similar.title: お〜ください
similar.explanation: Both can ask the other person to do something. 「お〜ください」 is a direct request, used for procedures and instructions; 「お〜いただけますか」 is a question and gentler, suited to making an extra request of a client.

similar.title: お〜願う・お〜願います
similar.explanation: Both are formal requests. 「お〜願います」 is mostly for announcements and notices addressed to many people (「ご協力お願いします」); 「お〜いただけますか」 is mostly for asking a specific person face to face.

similar.title: お〜する・ご〜する (humble)
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are 「お／ご」 + the continuative form. 「お〜する」 means my side does it for the other; 「お〜いただく」 means the other does it for me, so the doer is reversed.

formation: It is built from the honorific prefix 「お／ご」 + the verb's continuative form (or a Sino-Japanese action noun) + the humble verb 「いただく」. 「お」 + continuative turns the other person's action into a noun and adds respect (「お待ち」, 「ご確認」), and 「いただく」 is the humble form of 「もらう」, meaning “(I) respectfully receive.” Together: “respectfully receive the other's ‘waiting’ or ‘checking’,” i.e. “thanks to the other person doing …”. The doer is the other person and the receiver is my side, and that structure fixes the direction of meaning. Turning 「いただく」 into the potential question 「いただけますか」 means “may I receive your …?”, which makes a very polite request.

meaning: Honorific language. 「お + verb masu-stem + です」 concisely describes someone else's action or state, roughly equal to 「〜ている」 or 「〜する予定だ」.
connection: お + verb masu-stem + です; ご + Sino-Japanese action noun + です

senses.label: Ongoing・state
senses.meaning: Shows that the other person is doing something or is in some state. Equal to 「〜ていらっしゃる」.
senses.connection: お〜です. Common: 「お待ちです」, 「お探しです」, 「お困りです」
examples: The department manager is waiting for you in the meeting room.
Are you looking for something?

senses.label: Having・knowing
senses.meaning: Shows that the other person has something or knows something. 「お持ちです」 = 持っている, 「ご存じです」 = 知っている.
senses.connection: お持ちです／ご存じです
examples: Do you have a parking ticket?
Do you know Mr. Tanaka?

senses.label: Plans
senses.meaning: Shows what the other person is going to do. Equal to 「〜する予定ですか」; mostly used in questions.
senses.connection: お〜です／ご〜です. Common: 「お帰りです」, 「お出かけです」, 「ご出席です」
examples: About what time will you be back?
Will you be attending tomorrow's meeting?

senses.label: Arrival
senses.meaning: 「お見えです」 and 「お越しです」 mean a guest has arrived; they are honorific for 「来ている」.
senses.connection: お見えです／お越しです
examples: Your guest has arrived.
The company president will be coming in the afternoon.

notes: Use it only for the other person or a third party; for yourself it becomes self-elevating: ✕「私がお待ちです」→ ○「お待ちしております」; ✕「私もご存じです」→ ○「私も存じております」.
Only a limited set of verbs works, so don't apply it freely: ✕「お食べですか」→ ○「召し上がりますか」; ✕「お行きですか」→ ○「いらっしゃいますか」.
To outsiders, don't use honorifics for your own company's superiors: to a client don't say 「部長がお待ちです」; say 「部長の田中がお待ちしております」.

daily.title: At a shop
daily.description: A clerk greets a customer who comes in.
daily.example: Are you looking for something?

daily.title: At the station
daily.description: A ticket inspector asks a passenger.
daily.example: Do you have your ticket?

work.title: Reception notice
work.description: The receptionist calls a colleague to say a guest is waiting.
work.example: A guest is waiting for you at reception.

work.title: Informing your boss
work.description: A secretary tells the department manager a guest has arrived.
work.example: Sir, Mr. Tanaka has arrived.

etymology: The honorific prefix 「お／ご」 + verb masu-stem (used as a noun) + the copula 「です」. Describing the other person's action as a noun avoids naming the action directly, which makes it sound indirect and respectful.

similar.title: お〜になる
similar.explanation: Both describe the other person's action respectfully. 「お〜になる」 is the standard honorific, usable in any tense and for any action; 「お〜です」 is more concise and mainly expresses an ongoing action, a state or a plan (「お待ちです」 ≈ 「お待ちになっています」).

similar.title: 〜れる・〜られる (honorific)
similar.explanation: 「れる・られる」 attaches to almost any verb and shows lighter respect; 「お〜です」 shows more respect but is limited to a few verbs.

similar.title: いらっしゃる・おっしゃる (special honorific verbs)
similar.explanation: Verbs that have special honorific forms (行く・来る・食べる etc.) need those forms, not 「お〜です」; 「お見えです」 and 「お越しです」 are common honorific ways to say 「来る」.

similar.title: お〜する・ご〜する (humble)
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are 「お／ご」 + the continuative form. 「お〜です」 respects the other's action; 「お〜する」 humbles your own. 「お待ちです」 (they are waiting) and 「お待ちします」 (I'll wait) point in opposite directions.

formation: It is built from the honorific prefix 「お／ご」 + the verb's continuative form (nominalized) + the copula 「です」. A verb's continuative form can act as a noun (「待ち」, 「帰り」, 「持ち」); adding 「お」 makes it an honorific for the other person's action, and 「です」 asserts it, literally “(you) are in a state of ‘waiting’.” Presenting an action as a “state” rather than describing the action itself is indirect and respectful, so it mainly expresses ongoing actions, possession or plans. Because 「お」 respects the doer, this form can be used only for the other person or a third party, and only some verbs can be nominalized as 「お〜」, so not every verb fits.
